kakekotoba.interaction: よにあふ literally means 'to meet at night' but 世に逢ふ also carries the sense of 'in this world' — reinforcing the pun on Osaka (逢坂/逢う) that follows, so the phrase plays on both a nocturnal meeting and a worldly, ongoing state of affairs, echoing the poem's earlier night setting (夜をこめて) while pivoting toward the place name Ausaka.

Ausaka is simultaneously the actual Barrier of Ausaka (逢坂の関) on the road to the capital and the verb 逢ふ 'to meet' (as lovers) — the barrier that will not be crossed literally stands for the meeting the speaker refuses to permit.

はかる carries the sense of both 'to deceive/trick' (referring to the cockcrow ruse of the Han-ku story) and 'to reckon/scheme' — the fraudulent birdcall may deceive at the level of practical scheming, but it cannot overcome the deeper barrier.

jokotoba.text: 夜をこめて鳥の空音ははかるとも
jokotoba.function: The entire kami-no-ku recounts the Chinese legend of Meng Changjun's retainer who mimicked a cockcrow to trick the barrier guards into opening the gate before dawn — this extended narrative preface, longer than a single ku and freely composed for this poem, sets up the pivot into the Ausaka barrier by sound-association (empty birdcall vs. the guarded pass) and semantic contrast (a trick that works on one barrier but not on this one).

honkadori.source_poem: Meng Changjun's cockcrow anecdote from the Chinese Shiji/Zhanguo Ce (as known via Sei Shōnagon's own prose anecdote in the Makura no Sōshi and Chinese lore transmitted in Heian court culture)
honkadori.source_poet: Traditional Chinese legend of Meng Changjun (孟嘗君)
honkadori.function: Invokes the well-known tale in which a fake cockcrow tricked barrier guards into opening the gate at Kankoku Pass, allowing Meng Changjun to escape — the poem asserts that even such a clever ruse, which worked on that Chinese barrier, will not work on the Ausaka barrier of love/meeting.

kigo.note: The birdcall here refers to the legendary rooster's imitated crow of the Meng Changjun tale rather than a seasonal birdsong; it is emblematic/narrative rather than a natural seasonal marker. No other lexical item in the poem (barrier, night, meeting) carries a fixed seasonal association either — this is fundamentally a wit-poem built on wordplay and allusion rather than natural imagery, so no true kigo is present.

bipartite.kami_theme: The night-deep ruse of a false cockcrow, alluding to the Chinese legend of a barrier tricked open by an imitated rooster's cry
bipartite.shimo_theme: The declaration that the Ausaka Barrier — punning on 'meeting' — will never grant such easy passage, refusing the suitor's advances
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku sets up a precedent where trickery successfully breached a barrier, priming the reader to expect the same logic to apply; the shimo-no-ku overturns this expectation by asserting that the Ausaka barrier — which is simultaneously a real checkpoint and a metaphor for romantic 'meeting' (逢ふ) — cannot be fooled by the same ruse. The wit lies in the collision between a famous historical trick and the speaker's proud refusal, turning the whole poem into an elegant rebuff wrapped in scholarly allusion.

source_jp:
夜をこめて
鳥の空音は
はかるとも
よにあふさかの
関はゆるさじ
